deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published 1867). The page contains the end of Art. 10 and Art. 11. Notation: Ω = A_0 + A_1 + A_2 + ..., with A_n = A_n(x) = a_n cos nx + b_n sin nx. F is the twice formally integrated series, F(x) = C + C'x + A_0 x^2/2 − Σ_{n≥1} A_n(x)/n^2.

(a) End of Art. 10 (continued from the previous page). Let f be bounded and Riemann-integrable on [a, a+2π]. Split the interval into pieces of length 2π/n starting at a. On each piece, ∫ f(x) sin n(x−a) dx lies between (2/n)(m_s − M_s) and (2/n)(M_s − m_s). The reason is that sin n(x−a) is positive on the first half and negative on the second half, and ∫ |sin| over each half equals 1/n. Hence |∫_a^{a+2π} f(x) sin n(x−a) dx| ≤ Σ_s (2/n)(M_s − m_s) = (1/π) Σ_s δ_s D_s, where δ_s = 2π/n and D_s = M_s − m_s is the oscillation on the s-th piece. By Riemann's integrability criterion this sum → 0 as n → ∞. So the Fourier coefficients of a bounded integrable function tend to 0. This is the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma in Riemann's form.

(b) Art. 11 problem. Suppose the terms A_n(x) → 0 only at the given point x, not for all arguments. Reduce this to the previous case (Arts. 8–9, where all terms tend to 0).

Step 1. A_n(x+t) + A_n(x−t) = 2A_n(x) cos nt. So the series at x+t and x−t, added term by term, give 2A_0 + 2A_1 cos t + 2A_2 cos 2t + ..., a cosine series in t. Its terms tend to 0 for every t, because A_n = A_n(x) → 0.

Step 2. Define G(t) = C + C'x + A_0 x^2/2 + A_0 t^2/2 − Σ_{n≥1} A_n cos nt / n^2. Then G(t) = (F(x+t) + F(x−t))/2 wherever both series converge. This follows from cos n(x±t) and sin n(x±t) summed (my verification). G is the Riemann function of the series in Step 1.

I. Since the terms of the t-series tend to 0, the result of Art. 9 applies. Hence μ^2 ∫_b^c G(t) cos μ(t−a) λ(t) dt → 0 as μ → ∞, with λ a cutoff function as in Art. 9. This integral is the sum of μ^2 ∫ (F(x+t)/2) cos μ(t−a) λ dt and μ^2 ∫ (F(x−t)/2) cos μ(t−a) λ dt, if these exist. So the vanishing is governed by the behaviour of F at pairs of points placed symmetrically about x.

There must be points where the individual parts do not vanish; otherwise all terms of Ω would tend to 0 everywhere. At such points the contributions of symmetric points must cancel.

Marginal addition: if the set S of points where μ^2 ∫ F cos μ(x−a) λ dx does not tend to 0 is finite, Ω can converge only for finitely many x. These are midpoints of pairs from S (mod 2π). Only if S is infinite can a trigonometric series whose coefficients do not tend to 0 converge at infinitely many points.

Conversely, A_n = −n^2 (2/π) ∫_0^π (G(t) − A_0 t^2/2) cos nt dt. This holds because G − A_0 t^2/2 = const − Σ A_k cos kt / k^2 and ∫_0^π cos kt cos nt dt = (π/2) δ_kn. So A_n → 0 if μ^2 ∫ G cos μ(t−a) λ dt → 0 for every such localization.

II. If A_n(x) → 0, convergence of Ω at x depends only on G near t = 0. Specifically, A_0 + ... + A_n minus ∫_0^b G(t) (d^2/dt^2)[sin((2n+1)t/2) / sin(t/2)] λ(t) dt tends to 0, for b small. This is the symmetric form of the Art. 9 formula (sentence breaks off at the page end).

My derivation of the constant: (1/2π) ∫_{x−b}^{x+b} F(s) D_n''(x−s) ds = (1/π) ∫_0^b G(t) D_n''(t) dt, since D_n is even. Check: the term −A_k cos kt / k^2 of G against D_n'' = −2 Σ j^2 cos jt gives (1/π)·2A_k·π/2 = A_k.
errors: In II the constant before ∫_0^b G(t) D_n''(t) λ(t) dt appears as 2/π in the manuscript. Symmetrizing the Art. 9 formula (factor 1/2π over a symmetric interval) gives 1/π, and term-by-term checking confirms 1/π. This is probably a slip copied from the 2/π of the preceding A_n formula; the printed version, as I recall it, has 1/π.

The marginal claim 'only finitely many x while S is finite' is right but terse. It tacitly needs the cancellation to force S to be symmetric about x, so that x is a midpoint of two points of S, and it counts x modulo the period. The published text states the symmetry condition explicitly before drawing this conclusion.
The existence of the two partial integrals for F(x+t) and F(x−t) is assumed ('wofern diese Ausdrücke einen Werth haben'); no justification is given. This is acceptable as a heuristic remark.

results.what: Fourier coefficients of a bounded Riemann-integrable function tend to zero, proved via the oscillation sum over half-periods of the sine.
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Habilitationsschrift 1854, publ. 1867); Lebesgue 1903 for Lebesgue-integrable functions

results.what: Reduction of a series whose terms vanish only at x to a cosine series in t, by symmetrization; G(t) = (F(x+t)+F(x−t))/2.
results.modern_name: Symmetrization / Riemann's second integrated function and Riemann localization for series with non-null coefficients

results.what: A trigonometric series with coefficients not tending to 0 can converge only at points about which the 'singular points' of F are symmetric. Hence it converges at finitely many points if there are finitely many singular points.
results.modern_name: Precursor of the Cantor–Lebesgue theorem (convergence on a set of positive measure forces coefficients to 0)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (remark); Cantor 1870 and Lebesgue for the definitive theorem

results.what: Inversion formula A_n = −n^2 (2/π) ∫_0^π (G − A_0 t^2/2) cos nt dt, and the local partial-sum formula with the second derivative of the Dirichlet kernel.
results.modern_name: Riemann's localization principle for formal trigonometric series

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of Art. 10–11 of Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift, essentially matching the printed text. The only differences are minor wording, a marginal reformulation of the finiteness remark, and a probable constant slip (2/π for 1/π).

checkable.asserts: the polynomial part of G equals the average of F(x±t) (should be 0)
each half-period of sin n(x−a) has integral 1/n, giving the bound (2/n)(M−m) (here 1/3)
inversion A_n = −n^2 (2/π) ∫_0^π (G−A0 t^2/2) cos nt dt returns An
with n=5, the coefficient 1/π (not 2/π) in front of ∫ G D_n'' reproduces A_k for k≤n (k=3 shown; returns Ak)

transcription_corrections: In the definition of G the image appears to show a crossed-out '½' in front of A_0 xx; the intended term is A_0 xx/2, as transcribed.
In II the integral prefactor in the image is 2/π (as transcribed), not 1/π, but it is a slip.
In I the manuscript reads 'so muss μμ∫...' (the published text has 'so wird'); the transcription is correct here.
The upside-down note at the bottom right is unrelated to the derivation and largely illegible (it seems to mention 'Mannigfaltigkeit'); it is probably a fragment of other notes on the reused sheet.
The phrase 'Offenbar kann daher die Reihe Ω nur für eine endliche Anzahl von Werthen...' is a marginal addition in the right column continuing the main text, not part of the main column.
